justification: This is a re-check of the round-1 fixes, not a from-scratch re-derivation of the whole article; round 1 already verified every RFC quote, section citation, wire-format offset and independently-run program output byte-for-byte, and none of that content changed in this round's diff. I re-fetched RFC 8499 (section 6), RFC 3596 (section 2.1), RFC 5737 (sections 3-4), RFC 2606 (section 2) and RFC 1035 (section 4.1.1) myself for this round and confirm all five fixes are accurate. (1) Unsourced-claim fix: the opening paragraph's 'mixing up which side does which is the single most common way people get DNS wrong' is gone, replaced by 'Those are two different resolution styles, layered rather than interchangeable, and the rest of this article keeps them distinct throughout' -- no prevalence claim, sourced or not. (2) RA-clear scoping fix: the closing sentence of the recursive/iterative section no longer says 'root, TLD and authoritative servers all leave RA clear' as a category-wide absolute. It now says the root and TLD servers queried in the article leave it clear 'by design', that an ordinary authoritative server is 'normally no different, but RA is a per-server configuration flag, not a protocol guarantee that comes with being authoritative -- nothing stops a misconfigured server that also acts as an open resolver from setting it.' This matches RFC 1034 section 4.3.1's own framing of RA as a willingness flag, not a role-derived guarantee, and closes the round-1 finding exactly. (3) RFC 8499 section 6 attribution fix: the quote 'the first server pursues the query for the client at another server' is now explicitly attached to what RFC 8499 calls *recursive mode* ('RFC 8499 calls that single query a recursive query, and calls what the resolver then does on the client's behalf recursive mode: "the first server pursues..."'), not to 'recursive query' as round 1 flagged. I re-fetched RFC 8499 section 6 directly and confirmed that sentence is indeed part of the Recursive mode entry, and that the separate Recursive query entry is instead defined by the RD=1 bit -- the article's new wording is fully accurate and keeps both entries distinct. (4) RFC 3596 / RFC 5737 sourcing-hygiene fix: RFC 3596 is now in front matter (accessed 2026-09-22) alongside its existing inline citation for AAAA=28, and I confirmed on the live RFC 3596 section 2.1 that AAAA is defined there as type 28 verbatim ('The AAAA resource record type is a record specific to the Internet class that stores a single IPv6 address... value of the type is 28'). RFC 5737 now has a real inline citation in the failure-modes bullet ('RFC 5737 sets aside "for use in documentation", specifically so that addresses "SHOULD NOT appear on the public Internet"' with a link to section 3); I re-fetched RFC 5737 sections 3 and 4 and both quoted fragments are verbatim ('provided for use in documentation' in section 3 for the three TEST-NET blocks, 'SHOULD NOT appear on the public Internet' in section 4). Both round-1 sourcing gaps are closed. (5) Glue-IP guard: read the id=walk program directly. Before the (previously unconditional) `server = s.glueIp;` assignment, the code now checks `if (s.glueIp == "") { Console.WriteLine($"{hops[i]} referred us with no glue record"); break; }`. This correctly prevents the next loop iteration from calling `IPAddress.Parse("")`, which is exactly the unhandled-FormatException path round 1 flagged; the fix is structurally sound and the loop's early-break semantics (also used for `s.answerCount > 0`) are consistent with the rest of the function. I also re-derived the RFC 1035 section 3.2.2 and 3.3.x RDATA quotes behind the record-type table, which was reshaped in this round (columns merged, quotes shortened) -- every shortened quote ('32 bit Internet address', 'specifies the canonical ... name', 'specifies a host ... authoritative', 'willing to act as a mail exchange', 'one or more character-strings') still matches the live RFC 1035 text with the ellipses landing on genuinely elided words, not on anything that changes the meaning. I re-read the whole article fresh for anything else: the RFC 2606 quotes for .example/.test/.invalid/.localhost all check out verbatim against the live RFC; the RA-bit quote in the RD=1 exercise ('this be is set or cleared...', the RFC 1035 typo) still matches; the diagram-only edits (SVG text x-coordinates) and heading-text edits (e.g. 'The hierarchy below the root', 'A TTL controls caching, not propagation') are cosmetic/structural, not technical claims, and I did not find a new factual error or a new unscoped generalization anywhere in the diff or in the unchanged remainder of the article. run-code.mjs passed 6/6 consecutive runs with identical blocks=14 executed=6, confirming the harness sees no flakiness and the glue-guard addition did not change the executed-block count or break the walk program on the live network path it actually takes today (root -> .org referral -> iana.org referral -> CNAME answer, all with usable glue, so the new guard branch is not exercised on this page's happy path but is present and correct for a reader who edits the target name). What keeps this at 8.7 rather than higher: the RFC 5737 citation link anchor points only to '#section-3' while the prose attributes claims to 'sections 3-4' (a cosmetic mismatch, not a factual one -- both cited sentences are accurate and the reader lands on the right RFC page), and the article still asks a strong student to take on faith that 199.4.138.53 and the pechora*/iana-servers.net records shown as 'the run used for this page' will still be current when they read it -- an inherent property of live network content that dated captures and wildcarding already mitigate as well as they reasonably can.

issues.problem: The citation covers claims from both section 3 (TEST-NET-1 defined as one of three documentation blocks) and section 4 (the 'SHOULD NOT appear on the public Internet' language), but the link's anchor fragment only jumps to section 3. Not a factual error -- both quoted fragments are verbatim and accurately attributed to the RFC as a whole -- but a reader who clicks through lands one section short of the second quote.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either split into two citations, one per section, or drop the anchor fragment and link to the RFC's top so 'sections 3-4' isn't promising a jump the URL doesn't make.
